title: AI Mock — Paper 2 (Sections 9–12)
instructions: AI-generated Paper 2 style exam. All answers in Cambridge pseudocode. No programming language syntax. Calculators are not permitted.

questions.text: Which **computational thinking** skill involves ignoring unnecessary detail to focus on what matters?
questions.explanation: Abstraction removes irrelevant detail. Decomposition = breaking a problem into smaller parts; pattern recognition = spotting similarities.

questions.text: A program must calculate the wage of 200 employees. State **three** steps you would take to decompose this problem.

answer.text: Identify the sub-tasks: input the employee data (hours worked and rate of pay).
Calculate the wage for one employee (hours × rate, with overtime rules).
Repeat for all 200 employees and output/store the totals.

questions.explanation: Good answers name distinct sub-tasks that can be written as separate subroutines.

questions.text:
Perform a **linear search** for the value **11** in the array:

```
Index:   1    2    3    4    5    6
Value:   4    9    11   11   20   25
```

Complete the trace for the number of comparisons needed if the search **stops at the first match**.
questions.explanation: A linear search checks each item in order, so 3 comparisons are needed here. Worst case = n comparisons.

questions.text: A **binary search** is only valid when the data is:
questions.explanation: Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted list. Unsorted data cannot be split reliably.

questions.text: Write pseudocode for a **binary search** that searches for `Target` in a sorted array `Data` with 20 elements, and outputs the index if found or "Not found".

answer.text: Sets Low ← 1, High ← 20, Found ← FALSE
WHILE Low <= High AND NOT Found loop with Mid ← (Low + High) DIV 2
Correct three-way comparison: if Data[Mid] = Target set Found; if Target < Data[Mid] High ← Mid − 1; ELSE Low ← Mid + 1
Outputs index if Found, otherwise outputs "Not found"

questions.explanation:
Low ← 1
High ← 20
Found ← FALSE
REPEAT
    Mid ← (Low + High) DIV 2
    IF Data[Mid] = Target THEN
        Found ← TRUE
    ELSE
        IF Target < Data[Mid] THEN
            High ← Mid - 1
        ELSE
            Low ← Mid + 1
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
UNTIL Found OR Low > High
IF Found THEN OUTPUT Mid ELSE OUTPUT "Not found"

questions.text: A sorted array has **16** elements. What is the **maximum** number of comparisons a binary search needs?
questions.explanation: 16 = 2⁴, so at most 4 halvings are needed (log₂16 = 4).

questions.text: How many elements does the array `Values : ARRAY[1:10, 1:5] OF INTEGER` contain?
questions.explanation: 10 × 5 = 50 elements (a 2D array of 10 rows and 5 columns).

questions.text: Write pseudocode that reads 10 integers into an array `Nums`, then outputs them in **reverse** order.

answer.text: Declares the array: DECLARE Nums : ARRAY[1:10] OF INTEGER
FOR loop 1 TO 10 (or REPEAT/WHILE) to input each value into Nums[Index]
Second loop FROM 10 DOWN TO 1 (or FOR Index ← 10 TO 1 STEP −1)
OUTPUT Nums[Index] inside the second loop

questions.explanation:
DECLARE Nums : ARRAY[1:10] OF INTEGER
FOR Index ← 1 TO 10
    INPUT Nums[Index]
NEXT Index
FOR Index ← 10 TO 1 STEP -1
    OUTPUT Nums[Index]
NEXT Index

questions.text: When reading from a text file with `READFILE`, why is `EOF()` used?

options.text: To detect the end of the file so the loop stops at the right time

questions.explanation: EOF() returns TRUE when the end of the file is reached — used in WHILE NOT EOF(file) OR used with READFILE.

questions.text: A text file `scores.txt` contains one score per line. Write pseudocode to open the file, add up all the scores, and output the total and the number of scores.

answer.text: Declares the file and total/count variables; opens with OPENFILE "scores.txt" FOR READ
Loop WHILE NOT EOF with READFILE on the file
Adds each value to the total and increments the counter
Closes the file with CLOSEFILE and outputs the total and count

questions.explanation:
DECLARE MyFile : STRING
DECLARE Score : INTEGER
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
MyFile ← "scores.txt"
OPENFILE MyFile FOR READ
Total ← 0
Count ← 0
WHILE NOT EOF(MyFile)
    READFILE MyFile, Score
    Total ← Total + Score
    Count ← Count + 1
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE MyFile
OUTPUT Total, Count

questions.text: Which construct repeats a block of code a **known number of times**?
questions.explanation: FOR … NEXT is definite iteration (count-controlled). REPEAT/WHILE are indefinite (condition-controlled).

questions.text:
Rewrite the following **REPEAT … UNTIL** loop as a **WHILE … ENDWHILE** loop that does exactly the same thing.

```
REPEAT
    Sum ← Sum + Count
    Count ← Count + 1
UNTIL Count > 10
```

answer.text: WHILE Count <= 10
Sum ← Sum + Count

Count ← Count + 1
ENDWHILE

questions.explanation: REPEAT executes at least once and tests AFTER the body; WHILE tests BEFORE the body. The condition must be inverted.

questions.text: In the **program development life cycle**, what does the **analysis** stage produce?
questions.explanation: Stages: analysis → design → coding → testing → maintenance. Analysis defines client requirements.

questions.text: Explain the difference between **normal**, **abnormal** and **extreme** test data, giving one example of each for a program that inputs an exam mark from 0 to 100.

answer.text: Normal: data that should be accepted — e.g. 68
Abnormal: data of the right type but outside the acceptable range — e.g. 120 or -5
Extreme: the data at the boundaries of the range — e.g. 0 and 100 (also live/erroneous data such as 'abc' should be rejected)

questions.explanation: Extreme data = data at the very top/bottom of the valid range, which tests that validation uses > or >= correctly.

questions.text: A program is tested with every possible input value. Explain why this is **not** feasible and state what is done instead.

answer.text: There are too many possible values (e.g. all integers, all strings), so it would take far too long / is impossible to test every combination.
Instead, a test plan is used with representative data: normal, abnormal and extreme values.

questions.explanation: Also acceptable: it tests the boundaries and edge cases, plus black-box and white-box approaches.

questions.text: State what is meant by **maintenance** and give **two** reasons why programs need updating.

answer.text: Maintenance is the process of modifying a program after it has been released/implemented.
Reason 1: the user requirements or business processes change.
Reason 2: bugs/errors are found, or the system environment (hardware/OS) changes and requires updates.

questions.explanation: Types of maintenance: corrective, adaptive, perfective, preventive.

questions.text: Which is a **valid identifier** for a variable in Cambridge pseudocode?
questions.explanation: Identifiers contain only letters, digits and underscores, must start with a letter, and contain no spaces or hyphens.

questions.text:
Trace the loop and complete the table.

```
Total ← 0
FOR Count ← 1 TO 5
    Total ← Total + Count * 2
NEXT Count
OUTPUT Total
```
Explain why a **binary search** is faster than a **linear search** for a large sorted array.

answer.text: Each binary search comparison halves the remaining data (divide and conquer).
So it needs at most log₂n comparisons, whereas a linear search may need up to n comparisons — far fewer accesses for large n.

questions.explanation: For 1 000 000 items: linear ≈ 1 000 000 comparisons worst case, binary ≈ 20.
